title: Aromatic molecular emitters in a hexagonal boron nitride stack
authors: Tianyu Fang, Ricardo Gioia Alvarez, Babak Behjati, Moritz Scharfstädt, Max Masuhr, Bo Deng, Noah Henseler, Andrea Bergschneider, Stefan Linden, Christian Schäfer, Daqing Wang
abstract: Single polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon molecules embedded in organic matrices have proven to be an excellent family of narrow-linewidth quantum emitters. Extending this host-guest setting to van der Waals materials offers the opportunity to combine the preeminent properties of molecular emitters with the access to the versatility of two-dimensional hetero-structures and devices. In this work, we incorporate perylene molecules into multi-layered hexagonal boron nitride stacks and observe gigahertz-narrow zero-phonon-line transitions at cryogenic temperatures. We unambiguously verify the origins of photon emission through vibronic spectra analysis. By combining hyperspectral localization measurements with quantum chemistry calculations, we examine the insertion mechanisms of perylene molecules in the hexagonal boron nitride stacks, and conclude that pristine hBN layers tend to expel molecules from the sandwich, while extended morphological defects, hydroxyl groups and unpassivated boron and nitrogen atoms assist to stabilize molecular bindings to hBN. Our work provides valuable insight for future work to deterministically integrate narrow-linewidth molecular emitters into van der Waals devices.
summary: The research demonstrates the successful incorporation and spectroscopic characterization of perylene molecular emitters into hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) stacks. By analyzing narrow zero-phonon-line transitions and vibronic spectra at cryogenic temperatures, the authors confirm that while hBN offers a promising platform, molecular binding is critically dependent on structural defects rather than pristine lattice sites. This provides key guidelines for deterministically engineering such quantum emitter devices.
main_problem: To investigate the feasibility of directly embedding narrow-linewidth molecular quantum emitters (perylene) into van der Waals hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) stacks and characterizing their photophysical properties.
main_result: The study successfully observed gigahertz-narrow zero-phonon-line transitions, confirming that while pristine hBN tends to expel molecules, morphological defects stabilize the binding. The spectral analysis provides insights into the host-molecule interaction mechanism.
method: A combination of cryogenic optical spectroscopy (measuring ZPL and vibronic spectra) and advanced theoretical calculations (quantum chemistry/DFT) was employed for analysis.
model_or_system: The physical system is perylene molecules embedded within multi-layered hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) stacks, mimicking a solid-state quantum emitter platform. The analysis involves modeling excited-state relaxation and vibrational coupling between the molecule and the host lattice.
key_observables: Zero-phonon-line (ZPL) transition linewidth ($\approx 2.8\ 	ext{GHz}$), vibronic spectral peaks, phonon sideband shapes, and spatial mapping of emission intensity.
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperatures (e.g., 3.8 K); the electronic structure parameters derived from quantum chemistry calculations; defect concentrations in hBN.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that spectral matching techniques like LNCC can reliably identify molecular fingerprints even when broadened by the host environment, and that environmental stability is governed by surface defects rather than bulk properties.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate sample fabrication, compare fluorescence spectra from hBN vs. anthracene hosts showing vibronic peak agreement but sideband differences, and map ZPL wavelengths across samples to show spatial heterogeneity.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from initial characterization of the ZPL transition in the hBN stack, through detailed spectral comparisons with reference molecules (anthracene), to advanced techniques like LNCC matching for site-specific analysis, concluding with structural insights regarding molecular binding sites.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the integration challenge for solid-state quantum emitters by demonstrating high-fidelity optical characterization within a 2D van der Waals heterostructure, which is crucial for realizing scalable quantum devices.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Sample fabrication routine. An hBN flake is first prepared on a silicon wafer capped with a SiO2 layer. The substrate is then transferred into the evaporation chamber. After deposition, a second hBN flake is picked up by a polymer dome and stacked on the deposited hBN flake. The stack is picked up and transferred to a clean silicon substrate. (b) The sample is transferred to a closed-cycle cryostat, cooled to 3.8 Kelvin and studied under an optical microscope. Inset shows the molecular structure of perylene. (c) A simplified energy level diagram of perylene. The two images on the right side display the π-orbitals involved in the |S0⟩to |S1⟩transition.

Figure 2: Fluorescence spectrum measured from a focal spot on the hBN stack (a) compared to the emission spectrum of perylene in anthracene (b). The horizontal axis denotes the relative energy shift to the ZPL, expressed in inverse centimeters. The vibronic bands are scaled differently in intensity for visual effect. (c) Comparison to theory. The blue vertical bars in the top panel present the vibrational modes of perylene in an hBN slab. The height of each bar represents the Franck-Condon factors derived from ab initio calculations. Figure 3: (a) Emission spectrum measured on a laser focal spot on a non-baked sample over 200 seconds. (b) Extracted frequency traces of 6 molecules. Each molecule is represented by one color. The opaque lines denote the ZPL transition, and the semi-transparent lines are the vibronic transitions. (c) An emission spectrum measured on a sample after baking. (d) Extracted time traces of the ZPL and vibronic lines for the data in (c).

Figure 4: Fluorescence excitation spectra of the ZPL transition of a single perylene molecule. (a) The ZPL excitation traces measured with gradually increased laser intensities. The duration of a single frequency sweep was 12 seconds. The color scale is normalized in each scan. Spectral jumps occur at the highest excitation power. (b) Excitation spectra at each laser power. The gray dots show the accumulated data from (a) without post-aligning the center resonance frequency of each individual scan. The red lines denote fits to a Lorentzian function. The extracted full-width at half-maximum linewidth γ is given in the legend.

Figure 5: Spatial distribution of perylene emissions analyzed through hyperspectral mea- surements on two samples. (a), (e) Optical microscope images of the two samples. Orange and blue contours illustrate the boundaries of the lower and upper hBN flakes, respectively. (b), (f) Atomic force microscope measurements. The top and bottom flakes in (b) have a thickness of 21 nm and 31 nm, respectively. The sample in (f) has a 22-nm-thick bottom flake and a 2-nm-thick top flake. (c), (g) Integrated fluorescence intensity distributions. (d), (h) Normalized correlation function with respect to the emission spectrum of perylene.
